newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Congo's Sassou denies hiring Mobutu's troops.
newsitem.headline: Congo's Sassou denies hiring Mobutu's troops.

text.p: Congo-Brazzaville warlord Denis Sassou Nguesso on Wednesday denied charges of hiring mercenaries from the collapsed army of ex-Zaire dictator Mobutu Sese Seko.
The government of President Laurent Kabila, who toppled Mobutu in May, last month accused both sides in ethnic warfare in Brazzaville of recruiting former Mobutu soldiers.

But in a television interview broadcast across the river in Kinshasa, capital of the renamed Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sassou in turn accused President Pascal Lisouba, his rival in the Brazzaville fighting.
"The zone I control is open -- I challenge anyone to prove that there is one single member of Mobutu's former army there," Sassou told Raga Television.
He said if any ex-Zaire soldiers were involved in the Brazzaville conflict, they were fighting on Lissouba's side.

"If soldiers from Mobutu's army came to Brazzaville, they came before the war started. They were given hospitality by the presidency -- that's common knowledge. The generals were put up in hotels, the presidency knows just where," said Sassou, who ruled Congo for 12 years as a Marxist dictator.
Many senior Mobutu aides, civilian and military, as well as family members, fled Kinshasa through Brazzaville as Kabila's forces closed in after a seven-month guerrilla campaign.
Lissouba, who was a close friend of Mobutu, has been forced to gradually forge ties with Kabila after an initial reluctance to recognise the change of power in Kinshasa.
Three weeks ago Kabila's government threatened to take "military measures" against the warring sides in Brazzaville after accusing them of using defeated Zaire army soldiers.

Deputy interior minister Faustin Munene told reporters shells fired across the river Congo into Kinshasa since fighting broke out in early June in Brazzaville were the work ex-Zaire soldiers. The river separates the capitals of the two Congos.

International mediators holding talks with envoys of the two rivals reported progress in hammering a peace accord but a stumbling block remains Sassou's insistence that Lisouba relinquish power to an interim government.
The fighting has killed hundreds of people and devasted whole districts of Brazzaville and derialed plans for presidential elections last month. Both Sassou and Lisouba were due to contest.
More than 2,000 people died in Brazzaville in 1993 after election disputes sparked militia warfare.
